utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Is the next witness ready to go, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Mr. President, he is. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the courtroom. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As you know, first, the Prosecutor will conduct his examination-in-chief and will put questions to you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, again. Mr. President and good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I know you've testified before, and I just want to remind you that if there is anything I ask you that is unclear, to let me know so that I can restate it in a way that we can better understand one another and just to try speak a little bit more slowly than you would normally so that the interpreters have a chance to translate, interpret what you say accurately to the parties. Let me start by asking, do you recall testifying in the case of Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al, on 1st of June, 2007?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review your testimony before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And having reviewed that testimony, do you stand by it?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does it fairly and accurately reflect what you would say, were you to be examined here today and asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is nothing to add or subtract to what I said when answering the questions that were posed to me then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would offer into evidence, Mr. Simic's prior testimony as 65 ter 6588.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In addition to that, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 6588 shall be assign the Exhibit P2266.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In addition to that, Mr. President, I would offer into evidence the exhibits that were admitted through the witness in the prior proceeding. And those are 65 ter 6589, 6590 and 454.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: All three associated exhibits will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 6589 shall be assigned Exhibit P2267. 65 ter number 6590 shall be assigned Exhibit P2268. And 65 ter number 454 shall be assigned Exhibit P2269. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a brief summary of the witness's prior testimony I'd like to read into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Simic was born in 1952 in the village of Vrsac, Vojvodina, in the Republic of Serbia. He attended the University of Zagreb, earned a law degree and began his career in journalism in March or April 1975. Except for relatively brief periods, he worked continuously as an journalist. In 2002, Mr. Simic worked for weekly Belgrade publication called "Svedok." On 29th of October of that year, he published an article in "Svedok" featuring an interview with VRS Colonel Ljubisa Beara. A few months before Colonel Beara's indictment was made public, Mr. Simic considered interviewing him, particularly in light of his role and position at the time of the Srebrenica operation. Mr. Simic, who was then in charge editorially of army and security matters for "Svedok," used his connections to put him in contact with Colonel Beara, as he did not previously know him. After the indictment was made public, Mr. Simic intensified these efforts, and, through an intermediary was able to set up an interview with Beara, who agreed to it on three conditions: 1, that Mr. Simic come alone to the interview location; 2, that no photos were to be taken; and, 3, that Mr. Simic promise not to reveal the location of the interview. Mr. Simic interviewed Colonel Beara for about two hours, some two or three days after the indictment was made public. He used roughly 45 to 55 per cent of the interview material in the article, which included all the information Beara provided concerning the Srebrenica events, which, of course, was Mr. Simic's focus. Mr. Simic testified that he kept the article as authentic as possible, leaving Beara's responses as is, save for removing some filler words and repetitions. At its conclusion, Colonel Beara deadlined Mr. Simic's invitation to review the interview and Mr. Simic did not see Colonel Beara again. However, following the article's publication, the intermediary who had initially placed him in contact with Beara informed Mr. Simic that Beara was extremely satisfied with the article and had no objections to its content. Although during the course of the interview, Colonel Beara claimed, among other things, that he was not around during the Srebrenica events, that the VRS did not commit any mass crimes in Srebrenica, stating that this was "nonsense," and that he, Beara, was not -- was, rather, "convinced" that Srebrenica was engineered by the Muslims for propaganda purposes, Mr. Simic testified that it was his impression that Beara had been truthful during the interview. Mr. Simic also noted that, while he recorded the full interview, he was not able to locate or retrieve the tape, which may subsequently have been discarded or destroyed. This concludes my summary. And I do have some additional questions for Mr. Simic, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to have in e-court, please, P2269. This is the interview statement -- or, rather, the interview by Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Simic, do you recognise what we have here on the screen in e-court?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the title page of the issue of "Svedok" in which the interview with Mr. Beara was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to go to page 2 in the B/C/S. And we'll stay on the same page in the English, please. And can you tell us what we have here in this second page in the B/C/S language?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: That is one of the two pages containing the interview with Mr. Beara, as the interview was published on two pages of the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to go to page 7 in the English, and I think we'll have to go to page 3 in the B/C/S. And I have just a few questions regarding this. I'm sorry, for the English, we'll have to start at page -- no, we've got the right page. Towards the bottom of the page, you'll see a question that you put to Mr. Beara where you ask him: "Are you trying to say that the VRS did not commit mass crimes in Srebrenica?" Do you -- do you see that question?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in relation to that question, Mr. Beara, Colonel Beara responds at that they didn't, meaning the VRS didn't. And that The Hague allegedly had a list of mass grave locations. He says: "That they report there are 800 bodies in one grave, 2.000 in another, 3.000 in another." And he says: "They claim that they are primarily and secondary graves, alleging we moved the bodies." He says, "What nonsense." And that: "It is not possible to carry out such killings on a mass scale in the presence of UN representatives, even if someone had such an insane idea." And then he says: "In order to kill so many people in such a short time, one would need to engage a brigade?" Now, in terms of just that answer you recorded, was that essentially in the words of Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite certainly. Because, as can you see, the answer is very sensitive, and I do not think that Mr. Beara would not react and use the possibilities of the Public Information Act in Serbia if I had stated something wrongly or if I had interpreted his words wrongly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you're aware now, of course, that Colonel Beara was convicted of certain crimes in relation to these killings; are you not?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. But I'm not sure if the verdict has really come into force, if it's final or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you also are aware, are you not, that members of the Zvornik Brigade, in particular, have also been convicted in relation to their respective roles in the killings, mass killings of Muslims, regarding the Srebrenica events; are you not?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to take you to page 8 in the English of this article. And I'd like to focus you, if I could, on Mr. Beara's response to your question where you asked him: "Does it mean that Srebrenica was, in fact, engineered by the Muslims for propaganda purposes." Do you see it in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in response to that question, he says, as you've written in your article: "I am convinced it was. I don't know what the reason was, but it is monstrous to kill one's own people in order to spite someone." Then he talks about that that was the case in Markale. Do I understand from your article correctly that Colonel Beara's suggesting that the killings that occurred in relation to the Srebrenica events were perpetrated by the Muslims against their own?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, I did this interview with Mr. Beara in 2002, so that was eight or nine years ago, and I believe you understand that I cannot remember everything. But what I do remember, and what my impression was, are two things: Firstly, that Mr. Beara claimed that, at the relevant time, when the events in Srebrenica occurred, he was not in that location but, rather, in the Bihac area; and, secondly, he wanted to say, or prove, though he couldn't, but he kept insisting and claiming, and several times I omitted that because he kept repeating that everything had been engineered for the purposes of propaganda by the Muslims themselves. And if I can interpret him freely now, he said that there were some victims, but that the numbers were not at all the ones that were broadcast by the Muslim media and some international media in Europe and elsewhere in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say "victims," do you mean victims of the VRS; or when you say "victims," do you mean victims in the sense that the Muslims perpetrated the crimes against Muslim -- against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No, no. As far as I understood him, he said that there were victims but that their numbers were much fewer than the media claimed. And it is also true one can see that from the interview, I think that there is Mr. Beara's claim which is repeated twice in the interview, that the Muslims, or the Bosniaks, the members of their armed forces, came into mutual conflict and, as far as I remember, I think he also offered some proof of that and that that came, as far as I can tell, from a highly ranked French officer. He offered proof - that's what he told me and what I had published - that the Muslims, the members of their armed forces, had argued among themselves, had started fighting amongst themselves, and that there were some victims, as a result of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At the time that he told you this, during the course of the interview, was that your understanding of the events that had occurred back in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say how the events had developed because I was not in the area at the time. I had some information about events in Srebrenica, Zepa and Bratunac, and that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it came from media, what I saw on TV or read in the press. I had no reason not to trust Mr. Beara, especially as he seemed quite convincing. I could see that the accusations against him voiced by General Krstic, Vojislav Seselj, and some Muslim media were something that hit him really hard. And I remember that when he went away from his apartment that, on this occasion, he wanted to say his truth and his point of view about everything that occurred there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me take you to page 6 in the English. And we can see a question at the very bottom of page 6 in the English which is: "You participated in the operation of the Serbian forces entering Srebrenica?" Is a question. And we'll find the answer on the top of page 7 which is, I think in part, what you were just referring to were Colonel Beara's answer to you is: "No." And he says: "Nor did I know that it was being prepared," that is the operation of the Serbian forces entering Srebrenica. "My assignment was not to participate in preparing military operations. The operations Department of the Staff is in charge of that. I was involved in intelligence work. I was a counter-intelligence officer. When that operation started, I was on the Bihac front." Which is what you referred to; right? You'll have to answer for the record.

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He then says: "I returned when it was over," and says, "one day when I was taking mail to General Mladic, I saw a large number of buses on the road leading from Bratunac to Zepa and Srebrenica." And he says that: "The vehicles were sent from all over Bosnia to transfer the Muslims to Tuzla via Kalesija." He says: "An UNPROFOR convoy was providing security." And then he says: "Stories immediately started circulated in the press, even our own papers, of a crime and of mass killings of the Muslims." In relation to that, let me ask, first, did you ask him about his knowledge of the transfer en masse of these Muslims from Srebrenica? Did you ask him about that during the course of the interview?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I did not ask him such a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that because you considered the transfer of these individuals, of these people, en masse, from Srebrenica after the army had entered the enclave to be separate and apart from the Srebrenica operation, or for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: Not for that reason. When I look at the question and Mr. Beara's answer now, and that was also obvious when I testified in the Popovic case, I obviously did not do my work professionally, and I should have asked him an additional question when he said "one day." And it's not really clear what day it was when he saw those trucks or buses, whatever he mentioned. As for the transfer of these people in the convoys, I watched that on television. I know that that happened. Mr. Mladic was also there, as far as I can remember. And he guaranteed to the civilians, the women and children that nothing would happen to them. I can still see that picture in my mind because it was broadcast in the electronic media many times. However, it is obvious that Mr. Beara somehow disrupted my attention because I asked him where he was at the time, and he briefly responded that he was at the Bihac front and then he said that he had seen the buses and trucks. I did not sufficiently insist on that, for him to clarify that for me, when he was there. He said that he was carrying mail. He should have told me when he was carrying mail. That remained unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he share with you what he knew about this transfer of these individuals from the enclave? Did he tell you how it came about or who was involved in that, independently of you asking him about it? Voluntarily, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I recall, he didn't try to explain in any detail how those people were transferred. The women, the elderly, and children from Srebrenica to other locations. He didn't explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he say anything about the men that weren't transferred with those people, with the women and the children and some of the elderly? Did he tell you about what happened to the men that were also in the enclave and why they weren't transported out, together with the women and the children and some elderly? Did he mention that?

utterances.speaker: SREDOJE SIMIC
utterances.text: No. He did not discuss it in that way. I think that part of the interview was published, where Mr. Beara asserted that the unit of Naser Oric practically pulled out of Srebrenica and that they captured a Praga of theirs with a crew. He stated that the Bosniak officers asked to be let through so that the crew would not be harmed, and they were Serbs. I think he mentioned a corps, saying that that unit managed to get out of the encirclement. And he also said that General Delic himself inspected that unit in Tuzla following the withdrawal. I believe I mentioned that in the interview. It would mean that most of the able-bodied men who had arms managed to get out, and that was his assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now you can see in your article, itself, you, yourself, have written down that Colonel Beara said that: "Stories immediately started circulating in the press, even our own papers, of a crime and of mass killings of the Muslims." And you, yourself, mentioned just a moment ago that you were aware of some of these stories?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please move to that relevant part you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It is actually right on the screen. It's the last sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Oh I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a couple of articles. We'll start with 65 ter 7418. This is an article, Mr. President, that was not part of the Prosecution's original 65 ter list but is responsive, obviously, to the issues, both in the article itself and as per the witness's testimony because it concerns events that were published concerning the -- concerning the Srebrenica events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as you could probably see in our estimate we would need for the cross-examination of this witness, we reserved our right to place an objection for the OTP's request to include documents 65 ter 7416, 7418, and 7419 on the list. There is a number of reasons why we object. Before that, I just wanted to remind you that you are well aware of the practice of this Defence not to object to any new documents being introduced, in spite of the fact that some of them may not have been on the original 65 ter list. However, these are newspaper articles by Mr. Block and we see no basis due to which these documents should be put to this witness. First of all, there is no mention of them in the 65 ter summary of the Prosecution that they intended to use these articles. This witness's testimony is limited only to the circumstances under which Mr. Beara provided the interview and nothing more than. This witness's testimony in the Popovic case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I have to interrupt you. I would like to ask the accused, Mr. Tolimir, if he objects, and he may request that you address the Chamber. This is a bit beyond the normal proceedings, if you are raising such an objection. Mr. Tolimir, do you object to the addition of these three documents to the 65 ter exhibit list by the Prosecution? You may do that. This is your right. You can ask the Chamber to allow Mr. Gajic to address the Chamber. What is your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to greet all those present, and may these hearings be concluded in accordance with God's will and not my own. I would like to greet Mr. Simic. And I would kindly ask that no propaganda be admitted, and the witness testified to that effect. Now the Prosecutor is trying to have that admitted. If you believe it is necessary to have such material admitted, we could present a lot of Muslim books which also speak of events in Srebrenica, and we might ask for them to be admitted as well. I believe my legal assistant should be permitted to explain our Defence's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: just to clarify, we are not discussing the question, if these documents would be admitted into evidence. At the moment, we are discussing the request of the Prosecution to add them to their 65 ter exhibit list, which is a different matter. I understand your last sentence as a request to allow Mr. Gajic to address the Chamber on this topic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have a position to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please allow him to conclude his remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, in relation to the position of Mr. Gajic to address the Chamber, do you have a position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I do, actually. I think is entirely appropriate to add these exhibits to the 65 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, I asked you if have a position to the request of Mr. Tolimir to allow Mr. Gajic to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. No, I have no problem with that. If that's what he requires and would like, I would welcome it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The reason why I asked you, Mr. Tolimir, was the decision of the Chamber of the 28th of April, 2010. The Chamber decided that day that the audience of Mr. Gajic, the right of audience, is limited to addressing the Chamber on legal issues that arise during the proceedings upon a specific request for such, by the accused being granted by the Chamber. This is the reason why I interrupted Mr. Gajic, and the Chamber is of the view that Mr. Gajic should address the Chamber on this topic. I would like, first, to give Mr. Gajic the floor to continue with his objection. And then you may respond, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to apologise first for not having followed the prescribed procedure completely. In addition to what I've already said concerning the 65 ter summary for this witness, it is not clear from it that this witness was about to testify about the events in question. Another thing I wanted to object to is the following: Mr. Robert Block is neither on the witness list, nor can this witness, at least to the extent of our information, tell us anything about Mr. Robert Block, who authored the three articles that the OTP is now seeking to add to their 65 ter list. In our view, those articles have no probative value for the simple reason that they often refer to unidentified sources and they are nothing more than media reports published as such. Therefore, their probative value is basically none. I would conclude my arguments, having said that, and I hope I have sufficiently explained why we believe these documents should not be included on the 65 ter list at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gajic. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The first thing is that these documents are clearly relevant and probative of material issues arising out of the indictment. They are relevant and probative in respect of the fact that they were published. It's appropriate to put the fact of a journalistic publication about the events concerning Srebrenica to a journalist who, himself, authored such a publication, albeit many years after the fact, but throughout the period of time -- but worked as a journalist throughout that period of time up until the present day. It is entirely an appropriate issue to put to this witness. The second thing is that the fact of publication or the information that was available in the media during and around the time of the events in question is directly referred to in his article. It's referred to in the paragraph that I just read into the record, where, during the course of the interview, Colonel Beara, himself, makes reference to media reports concerning crimes and other events related to the Srebrenica operation. Not only that, but the witnesses, himself, said during the course of his testimony today that he, himself, was aware of certain reports concerning the Srebrenica events at the time. And so I think it is appropriate in these circumstances to put these documents to the witness: First, to see whether or not the witness is aware of the fact that these documents -- that these stories were published; and, secondly, as to the content. That is, what was published. It doesn't go necessarily to the truth of the matter that this fact happened or that fact happened, but what it goes to is the question of what was being reported about Srebrenica, true or untrue. That is of relevance to this witness's testimony and also of relevance to the accused's knowledge of these facts, to the general knowledge in the VRS about these facts. Remember, we have witnesses who have testified here ranking as high as the chief of -- of intelligence in the VRS who have claimed not to have any knowledge of three events. And so it is a salient issue of relevance to these proceedings and entirely appropriate to put to this witness as is mentioned in his article and is the subject matter of his testimony today. Mr. Gajic says that this was not part of the 65 ter summary, in particular. But what is part of the 65 ter summary, undoubtedly, is the article itself that he wrote. And what is part of that article, indisputably, is that he reported that Colonel Beara said that there were media reports concerning the Srebrenica events as he wrote down in the article, so it is an entirely appropriate avenue to pursue. And that's the reason why I think it is appropriate to add it to the 65 ter list, to show it to the witness. Ultimately, the Trial Chamber will determine whatever weight to give it, if it decides to admit them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To understand your position better, I would like that ask you: All the three articles were published in "The Independent" newspaper; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And all three articles were published in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you are saying that you want to show, by using these documents, that there have been -- yes, some news articles about the Srebrenica events at the relevant time?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would briefly touch upon one thing that the Prosecutor said. Namely, the article that is the core of this witness's testimony is an interview, basically, which understands recording the words of another person; in this specific case, of Mr. Beara. In the article, there is no comment made by the witness. He did not go into analysing those events or anything that had to do with Srebrenica. This was simply conveying information uttered by someone else. When making your decision on our objection, I would kindly ask you to bear that in mind as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just as a clarification from you, Mr. Vanderpuye, where is the journalist, Robert Block; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't know off the top of my head. I think he is in the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did want to add one thing that I think may be of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The first thing is that I've -- I've learned, since you've started debating the issue, that Mr. Block is in Florida in the United States. The second thing I should point out to you, I think, which is important is that these are public documents. In other words, if you type in his name in the Internet, you'll get these articles. A number of these documents have been disclosed already to the Defence, despite the fact that they're public, as late as April of 2010. So this is not a surprise to the Defence or inaccessible to the Defence. Indeed, when I was preparing the binder for this witness, I was able to find these articles on the Internet, as recently as a couple of days ago, Thursday or Wednesday of last week. So it seems to me that this is not something that the Defence could not have reasonably anticipated, particularly in view of the fact that the article itself mentions publications soon after the Srebrenica events. So as a matter of notice, it seems to me that the Defence is clearly on notice of this issue, certainly if not specifically to this accused, then more generally in the case. And it has arisen, as I mentioned before, with respect to the knowledge of these events, as has been testified to by other witnesses in this case, including, intelligence officers and security officers, as well as people that were actually on the ground. And can I point to the transcript in respect of this issue, specifically with relation to one witness, if the Trial Chamber would like to -- to develop that or like me to elaborate on that further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To clarify the matter, I would like to ask the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: given to the Prosecutor, do you remember having seen on TV or in the media any reports about the events in Srebrenica in July 1995 in Serbia? Did you -- did you say anything about that during your examination today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to clarify one thing about 1995. I started working as a journalist in Serbia in May of -- or April of 1995. That is to say, a month and a half before Operation Flash in Croatia. I had not worked for over two and a half years prior to that. I was in Vrsac staying with my uncle for private reasons which are irrelevant for my testimony. Now, whether, in 1995, and in what month I heard or saw or read anything about Srebrenica is difficult for me to say. But I need to say the following: As time went by, there was more and more information by way of newspaper articles, broadcast programmes and content in the electronic media, depending on the source. The case of Srebrenica was very interesting for all of us living in western -- western Balkans; that is to say, in the successor states of the SFRY. There were such texts authored by Zagreb editorial rooms and Bosniaks had their own view. The Serb media in Bosnia-Herzegovina had their own; whereas, for Serbia, the media were divided. One club reported on the issue of Srebrenica one way, and the other in another way. There was much confusion. I saw many programmes about Srebrenica and read many articles, but I can't tell you who wrote what and in what newspaper. That would be very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that explanation. Mr. Vanderpuye, Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Gajic, the Chamber has considered your request to add these three documents to the 65 ter exhibit list, but the Chamber is not persuaded that the -- that you have laid a good foundation, a convincing foundation for this request. We -- in the past we had several occasions when you requested such an addition to the 65 ter exhibit list. There was no objection by the Defence and, therefore, in most cases, we granted this addition. Today, the Defence put the objections to the Chamber, and the Chamber is of the view that we don't see a connection to the current witness, the witness here present in the courtroom. There may have been quite a lot of articles in the world. These are three articles in "The Independent" newspaper, published in another state and not in the region. The witness can't testify about these articles. He just explained further what he said earlier on page 8, lines 10 to 12, that there were different media at the relevant time, even in the region, but with different sources and different information. The Chamber is not of the view that this witness is the right witness to put additional media articles from another part of the world and to testify about the existence of these articles or of the content of these articles. This is the reason why we will, in this case, not grant your motion. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do understand -- I understand the Court's point of view. I do have -- nevertheless, I do have an article that has already been admitted in this case by the same author, whom I think it would be appropriate to put questions to this witness concerning the content of this article. There are a couple of issues. One is to establish whether or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please indicate which article you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have P1254.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which -- through which witness did you tender it and we have received it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just a moment I'll find out for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told it was a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. PW-063, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This article on the screen is in evidence, as P1254. You may put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic what we have here is an article, as can you see that is written by -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What we have here is an article, Mr. Simic. It's dated 25th July 1995. And it's entitled: "River killings shed light on scale of horror after the fall of Srebrenica." And it says, "By Robert Block, Loznica, Serbia." In the first paragraph of this article, we see some discussion about an individual who Mr. Block writes is a person by the name of Resid Halilovic and he talks about this individual throughout the article. In the second paragraph, it says that: "On the 15th of July, four days after Bosnian Serbs overran Srebrenica, Mr. Halilovic was discovered lying in the shallow water of the Bosnian side of the Drina river," and he was badly bleeding and screaming for help. First, have you heard about what we've gone through so far? Did you hear about that in or around July 1995?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question, because I actually do not remember. This first and last name seemed to exist in my subconscious, but I cannot place them anywhere specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Throughout the article, you will see that this individual was apparently treated in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page. And I think we'll have to go to the second page in the B/C/S as well. It may be the last -- second-to-last paragraph in the B/C/S, but it reads that: "The officials of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in Belgrade say they are aware of several cases of Muslims from Srebrenica who fled across the Drina to Serbia only to be handed back to the Bosnian Serbs and an uncertain fate. Thousands of men from Srebrenica were taken prisoner by the Bosnian Serbs after their 'liberation' of the Muslim enclave on 11 July. Some estimates of prisoners executed are as high as 4.000." Now, you can see that this was reported from Loznica, Serbia. It also refers to officials of the UNHCR in Belgrade who make these statements. And my question to you is: Were you aware of the facts and circumstances as reported in this article in or around July 1995.

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: No. Certainly not in July 1995. Because I already said in 1995, in March or April, I started working in Belgrade. For three years before that, I was unemployed and was not working as a journalist at all. Later on, in some newspapers from Sarajevo, or excerpts from these articles and from these media which were quoted by some Belgrade papers, I saw such stories. Namely, that the Bosniaks who had crossed the Drina into Serbia were sent back. Even that some of them were provided with medical assistance, if they were injured, at the medical institutions in Serbia. I was reading about that for years, but I did not really investigate that or pay special attention to it. So I really cannot say anything specific about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you one other question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can go back to page one of this document and the fourth paragraph of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It says that: "In the days after Srebrenica fell, residents reported seeing 'truck loads' of men being brought to shallow pits dug on the other side of the river bank and shot by Bosnian Muslim [sic] soldiers. 'Dozens of people stood on a hill here and watched this,' said one Serb from the area who did not want to be identified. 'Last week I saw, with my own eyes, 50 men shot as they were forced to jump off the back of a truck into a pit.'" And my question is the same to you: Were you aware of the facts and circumstances as reported in this article back in July of 1995? Is this among the stories that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: It seems similar to one of the stories which I read in the Bosnian and partly also Croatian media. But what was really happening, what the truth was, that is something I do not believe I am an adequate witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just interested to know what you heard about, or what you heard was reported around that time. And you've indicated - and correct me if I'm wrong - that this is, or these represent some of the things that you heard about in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: As for the events in Srebrenica, Zepa, and the area along the Drina in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that was something that the Serbian media reported little about in 1995; and when they did, it was rather brief. Later on, as time went by, and as some non-governmental organisations and individual media dealt more seriously with the truth about Srebrenica and began to investigate it, there were many more articles published in the press. From Serbian, Bosnian and even some Macedonian and Montenegrin sources, many articles were published which also dealt with crimes against the Serbs; also in Bosnia and in the vicinity of both Srebrenica and Zepa. It happened more than once that in a newspaper, you would have an article on half a page, or even a full page, discussing what happened to the Bosniaks from Srebrenica; for example, quoting sources from the Zagreb or Sarajevo media. And on the other page; for example, on the right page, would you have a whole page including the testimony of a Serb who suffered or whose family perished or a report about the perishing of Serbs in villages surrounding Srebrenica. So in one and the same newspaper, there were both kinds of articles. I did not really deal much with the crimes committed in Bosnia and Herzegovina, just a little about what happened in Croatia because that was where I used to live before the war. But as for this subject, Srebrenica, and, in particular, this period that you insist on, Mr. Prosecutor, I mean 1995, a lot of time has passed since, almost 15 years, and at the time I was just beginning to work again as a journalist, and I had all kinds of problems. So perhaps I could say that, at the beginning, in 1995, 1996, 1997, I didn't really pay that much attention to Srebrenica and what was reported about it because there was so much information. This happened, that happened. Then a fortnight ago, it would turn out that it wasn't true. They would report that somebody had gone missing or had been killed, and then he would appear later on and it would turn out that he was alive. On the other hand, I was more focussed on Croatia, because many of my family members stayed there. My brother, who is now in Slovenia, was wounded at the time and because of that, I also had to leave Croatia. So I was preoccupied with some other private problems and did not deal with this too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I think the witness repeated now several times what kind of knowledge he had at the relevant time. You received the answer he could provide you with, and you should move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's where I'm going, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Very good. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic in your answer you represented, or you said, rather, that you considered Serbian media in respect of the issues that I've asked you about. And my question to you is -- and you can hopefully answer it directly, is: Did you consider other sources of information concerning the events in Srebrenica besides Serbian media? And you can answer yes or no and that probably ought to suffice.

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you consider any of this media in respect of the interview that you conducted with Mr. Beara in 2002, in order to prepare for it, for example?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so when Mr. Beara made the reference to stories that circulated immediately after the Srebrenica operation, do you have any idea what he was referring to, what stories and from what sources?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I did not understand Mr. Beara properly or if you have not understood me properly. Mr. Beara said that he was surprised when General Krstic linked him to Srebrenica, not only him but some other officers of the VRS. However, he said -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm referring to what Colonel Beara told you about crimes and mass killings of the Muslims, that you refer to in the English of page 6 and 7 of your article, where you say that Mr. Beara said that stories immediately started circulating in the press "even our own papers," which I take it to mean Serbian papers, "of a crime and of mass killings of the Muslims." What did you take that to mean? What papers, what press, and what sources?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: Well, there, he talked about the Serbian newspapers and the Serbian media, as far as I understood him. At the time, in the 1990s, up until the 5th of October, some of the newspapers were state-owned and were under direct control of the regime. When crimes or incidents occurred, they were rather weary and they offered only selective information. However, already at the time, there were many independent privately owned media which reported much more freely. They would use more sources, and sometimes even quoted or took over reports of other media from the region. So that when Mr. Beara said that the first number of the victims that was mentioned was 14- to 16.000 men and boys, he probably meant that the Serbian newspapers reported about that. And that is true, what he said at the time, that all sorts of information was published. But it is also true that as time went by, the number was diminished, and then, most often, the one that was mentioned was 7.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So the reports of crimes that were circulated immediately after the Srebrenica operations was information that you, yourself, were aware of at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of it in 1995, 1996, 1997, and as time went by, I knew more and more because more information became available even to ordinary people and, in particular, to the journalists. But I have to say that confusion reigned at the time. For two or three months, one information was reported about. Then, on another occasion, there would be some different information or a third piece of information, depending on the source, and it created confusion among the people. The people did not really what was actually happening. And even us, the journalists, we didn't know what the truth was or what happened at some points.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I take it that you're aware that Colonel Beara was convicted concerning his involvement in the murders of thousands of Muslim prisoners in July 1995 following the Popovic trial in which you testified. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This question is already answered, if I'm not mistaken, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Simic added that he is not sure about, if this is the final sentence. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not certain if it is an error, I'm looking at the record just now, I think that Mr. Vanderpuye was translated as if he said that the judgement against Mr. Beara was final. But Mr. Vanderpuye didn't say that because, as we know, the appeals proceedings are underway in this case at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see the word final in the transcript. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that was how it was interpreted into Serbian, and as it was a question that the witness was asked, I had to intervene because the witness, himself, said that he was not sure whether the judgement was final or not, so I just wanted to make sure that this is clear in the Serbian language as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Knowing what you do now, Mr. Simic, and given Mr. Beara's conviction, do you still believe that he told you the truth during the course of your interview with him in 2002?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: Well, I still believe what I believed then. He made an impression on me as a man who was speaking the truth. Especially as regards several occasions that, at the relevant time, he was not in the Srebrenica area but, rather, in the Bihac area; that he had great difficulties only after Mr. Vojislav Seselj had publicly attacked him in the media; that he had many problems and was concerned about his family; and that after 35 or -6 years as serving as a honourable officer, as he said, that this all hit him hard and considering all the circumstances, the impression he left with me was that he was saying the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. I don't have any questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That concludes my direct examination, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vanderpuye. Now it is your turn, Mr. Tolimir, to commence your cross-examination. Would you prefer to start immediately or would you like to have the break now and then commence your examination after the break? It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can take the break so that we do not disrupt the continuity of questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine. Sir, we must have our first break now, and we will resume after approximately half an hour. I think five minutes past 4.00 should be convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Now you may commence your cross-examination. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Once again, I wish to greet everyone present and I hope that this day ends in accordance with God's will rather than with my wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I wish the witness a pleasant stay among us and a pleasant return back home.

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: During the cross-examination [as interpreted], on page 71 [as interpreted], and the towards the end on page 31, you were asked whether you know -- on page 71, whether you know that Beara was convicted for crimes that have to do with these killings. And on another page you say: "Knowing that Beara was convicted, do you still believe that he was telling the truth?" My question is this: Do you know that Beara has been convicted only from the media, or do you have any specific information or proof on the basis of what he was convicted, or do you know this only from the media?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: That Mr. Beara was convicted, but I said I'm not sure whether it is final or not. I have heard that from the media, that is to say, from an agency, piece of news, because there are two news agencies which reported about this in Serbia, "Beta" and "Tanjug," not just about Mr. Beara but everyone who was in the preceding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you made a reference to page 71 of today's transcript, but we have only reached page 33. I think that was slip -- yeah. You made a mistake. I think you were referring to page 31; is that correct? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the first reference mentioned by Mr. Tolimir was 7, page 7, but the line was 1 or 2. And after that, I think it has been recorded properly. After that, page 31 was mentioned. So these are two separate references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Go ahead, please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 7, in line 19, the question was this: Does that mean that you know that Srebrenica was Muslim propaganda? On page 7, 24, you said Beara was the one who said it was all Muslim propaganda, that there were some victims, but that the numbers were not those reported by the Muslims in their media, more or less. I'm paraphrasing now what you said. This is my question: Was it during a long period that this was the media image created by the media, as the one that Beara talked about here in three different ethnic communities.

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: It was roughly as Mr. Beara put it. There's Serbian media, the majority of them at least, not all, though, not all, claimed -- or, rather, hinted that this was Muslim propaganda. Whereas, the Muslim and some of the Croatian media claimed that this was a crime without precedent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 8, line 12, you said: "He said that there were some victims but much fewer than reported in the media. He said that the Muslims had argued among themselves and fought among themselves and that there were some casualties as a result of that and that he offered information about this to French officers." Was that so? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: Yes, that was what Mr. Beara said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question -- I apologise to the interpreters. My question is this: Did the Muslim media also contribute to this view an opinion on the Serbian and Muslim sides by their reports about the number of casualties and how they were offered that some Muslims should be killed so there would be an intervention? Did you have sort of information and was something like that circulated in the public? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: The Muslim, that is to say the Bosniak media, let me say, insisted on the story about genocide, crime, and a huge number of casualties. That was accepted by many non-governmental organisations, even in Serbia. And a greater part of the international public also referred to Srebrenica as a crime. It's something that was final, that the crime occurred there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can we now please see 1D53 so that we can first see how the Muslim side reported about this in June 1998. Once we have a look at this, I will ask you my question. Thank you. This is an interview with Hakija Meholjic, who was a member of the War Presidency of the Srebrenica, and at the same time he was the president of the SDP for Srebrenica. It's the second strongest party. And he says: "500 [as interpreted] Muslim lives for military intervention." He published that in newspapers in Sarajevo, in Bosnia, called "Dani" on the 22nd of June 1998. And he says, the journalist asks him: "In your accusations of the state leadership, and particularly of President Izetbegovic, over a share of the Bosniak blame for the Srebrenica tragedy, the departure of the Srebrenica delegation to Sarajevo in September 1993 for talks on the fate of this enclave cannot be avoided?" I have read the introductory question which the journalist asked. Now I will only read a part of what Mr. Meholjic said in the fourth line from bottom up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, just to have a clear record, on page -- I don't know if it is a translation issue or if you made a mistake. On page 35, line 14, you are recorded as having said, "500 Muslim lives for military intervention." If you look into -- on to the document on the screen, you see in the document we see the figure of "5.000 Muslim lives for military intervention." If you would agree to that, then you should continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It is as you said, and is as it says here in the English version. And Meholjic then says in the first paragraph - I'm reading from the bottom - the last five lines, what is under quotation marks. I quote: "What do you think about the swap of Srebrenica for Vogosca? There was a silence for a while. And then I said, Mr. President, if this is a done thing, then you should not have invited us here, because we have to return and face the people and personally accept the burden of that decision." This is my question: Was there any information in the public, both ours and the Muslim ones, that Srebrenica was to be swapped for Vogosca and that the swapping was -- or had been announced since 1993, as Meholjic says here. Were you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: One could hear such rumours, especially in the then-opposition papers or from opposition leaders in Serbia as well as among certain VJ officers. I heard such stories a number of times in different versions, one of which is was the one you have just referred to. I can't specify what year exactly it was, though. In any case, I know of that option, although I don't know how accurate or true it is. I didn't see this interview before, although I know this Hakija and I know the editorial staff of this newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes. It seems that in the "Dani" newspaper it is stated that he refused Izetbegovic's offer, and then I quote his answer: "We rejected it without any discussion. And he said, you know, I was offered by Clinton in April 1993, after the fall of Cerska and Konjevic Polje, that the Chetnik forces enter Srebrenica, carry out a slaughter of 5.000 Muslims and then there be will be a military intervention." My question is this: Did you also hear such stories in the media on both sides, and did you know that -- gave an interview, this Mr. Meholjic gave an interview to the "Dani" newspaper?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: I don't know whether any Bosniak media reported on this. It is the first time I see it. I don't remember any Belgrade papers carrying this interview unless I missed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's going to be page 2 of the interview. Let's see what Meholjic says further about Srebrenica in 1995. He was a War Presidency member: "When Srebrenica fell in 1995, you had a chance to address President Izetbegovic?" That was the journalist's question. And in the second paragraph, Meholjic answers: "I requested then that a state commission be formed to examine the responsibility of the international community, the president, the Army General Staff, the 2nd Army Corps, our responsibility. The people are missing, he (President Izetbegovic) asked me what I would achieve by doing that. Rasim Delic tried to say something too. But nobody gave him a chance to speak." Did you hear or did you know that the Muslims demanded political responsibility and accountability by their state leadership for the events in Srebrenica? Did you know anything about that from the media?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: The Serb media reported that, quoting some media from Germany, I believe, or German language newspapers in any case, as having mentioned such requests. The problem was that such information was not always taken seriously; at least that was my feel of things in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said that Beara mentioned those clashes between the Muslims, the Prosecutor asked you whether, indeed, events took such a turn. And then you stated: "I had no reason to distrust Beara, and I believe the accusations levelled against him were the reason why he decided to give me an interview." My question is this: When we read these articles today, could we form the same conclusions you did at the time? That is to say, that Beara was personally accused of something that even the Muslim media blamed on some Muslims as carried by the Serbian media?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: When I tested in the other case, I said the same thing. It was my impression, as a human being not as a journalist, that Mr. Beara was bitter because of everything that was going on. Perhaps it may be important to say that when the Law on Co-operation with The Hague Tribunal came into force in Serbia, a list of indictees was published for Srebrenica. At the time, Mr. Beara was not on the list. His name appeared subsequently, and he constantly claimed that that was because he had come into conflict with paramilitary formations of Mr. Seselj in Montenegro concerning a barracks which was within his area of responsibility. At the time, he did not allow for something to take place. There seems to have been an incident there. In short, it seems he did not allow those paramilitary members to kidnap -- or, rather, to -- to seize military combat vehicle. Following that, Mr. Seselj kept attacking Beara in the media, stating that he was a liar and it bothered him a lot. It also bothered him what the Bosniak media wrote about him, stating that he was basically the -- a brain behind everything that took place in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have this admitted and then move to another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many pages does this document have? Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This document contains four pages. Not even four. But, yes, half of the fourth page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D53 shall be assigned Exhibit D277. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. D268, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We will see that even the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina published documents mentioning a high number of victims. For example, let's look at this document from the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its State Security Service; its Tuzla sector. Let's took at paragraph 7 where it says: "In further conversation, Enver stated that when the 285th and 282nd Brigade came out at around 10.00 on the same day, a Chetnik paramilitary formation opened artillery fire on the remaining brigades and civilians who happened to be at Buljin. In his estimate, around 1.000 civilians and soldiers were killed there."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "... so according to his estimate, some 1.000 soldiers and civilians were killed there." Without referring to some other statements which mention these events involving some suicides and murders, my question is this: Can we see from it that there were also casualties during combat, en masse? There are five statements in total which refer to the same location; and was there any information in the public that there were numerous casualties sustained by the units attempting to break through?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: I think I have partially answered it when responding to the Prosecutor's question. Mr. Beara said as well that a number of Muslim fighters were killed in mutual conflict or in mutual fights. This was not the first time I heard of it. Such information were in circulation even before he told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at D269, which refers to the same event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... now it works. The last document and this one don't have an English translation yet. They are both marked for identification, pending translation. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see another document by the authorities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from its state security sector. They received a statement from a specific person whose name I won't mention. It was marked as state secret and forwarded to their leadership. Let's look at page 2 of the document. Let's look at line 12: "The source states that, on that occasion, some 1.000 soldiers and civilians from the column were killed. After the crime, the Chetniks invited the people to surrender or to negotiate. On that occasion, Ejub Golic talked to the Chetniks, asking that the shelling be stopped. They, indeed, did so. They stopped shelling the columns of civilians and soldiers. After the shelling stopped, the 284th Brigade gathered in the nearby woods and continued en route to the free territory." Can we see from these two statements that they actually refer to this location at which around 1.000 soldiers and civilians were killed in combat; and did you know that all these victims and all other combat casualties were counted as people who were executed by firing squad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think the last part of General Tolimir's question gravely misstated the evidence before this Trial Chamber. I don't know exactly why he would ask a question like that, given the evidence we have here. Maybe he has something else in mind. But there's been no evidence in this case that these thousands of individuals that are referred to in this document, or any other document, were counted among the victims of the mass killings or in mass graves in this case. There's just no evidence of that. In fact, to the contrary. We've heard the evidence of Mr. Janc who carefully and conscientiously explained exactly how these victims were counted or considered in terms of the overall victim population concerning the Srebrenica events. So I'd ask General Tolimir to either restate that question or ask a different one because it unfairly misleads this witness and mischaracterises the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you give us a reference to that statement you gave in the last question when asked the witness: "Did you know that all these victims and all other combat casualties were counted as people who were executed by firing squad?" To whom are you referring? Who was counting them as victims of executions? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm looking for the reference to which Mr. Janc referred to when he said that they were all considered genocide victims. All those in the various mass graves were considered as genocide victims. By your leave, I will find it. I can go back through my notes and provide you with an exact reference. If you want me, I can do that now, or I can forward it to you later. In any case, Mr. Janc said during his testimony that he considers all such victims, genocide victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, in your question, you didn't refer to mass graves. Now you are referring to those found in mass graves. This is different. I propose that you rephrase your question and we can overcome this difficulty.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Babic [sic], did you know that 7.000 people were -- are believed to be the victims of genocide and this is something you also referred to in your testimony, I believe?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is not Mr. Babic but Mr. Simic. Please provide us with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, it's no problem. There were different pieces of information in circulation among the public. I don't know which one is correct. And I don't know whether the victims were actually ever counted in the area of Srebrenica. In Serbia at least, and in its neighbourhood, there are different NGOs who came forth with certain numbers that were carried by the media. In Serbia, in any case, such figures are usually in the area of 7.000 civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for calling you Mr. Babic, Mr. Simic. Let us now please look -- as we will not be discussing this anymore, I just wanted to provide an example as to how everything is subsumed under victims of genocide. Can we now please see the document D176. While we're waiting for it to appear on the screen, we'll say -- here it is. It's a document from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, their 2nd Corps command from Tuzla, which talks about the chronology of events --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is there an English translation? There should be one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have it on the screen. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a document from the 2nd Corps command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina issued on the 27th of July 1995; that is to say, immediately after the events. And the title is: "Chronology of events surrounding the break-through by the 28th division." Sent to -- it was signed by Sead Delic, brigadier, commander of that corps. On page 12, line 2, you said, and I quote your words: "Beara claimed that Naser Oric's unit had pulled out, that they had taken a Praga and that this unit was reviewed and that most of them managed to leave the area." That is what you said on page 12, line 2. Let us see what the Muslim sources say about this. So can we please show page 7 in the English version of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the accused please repeat the page references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please give us, again, the page reference. You said page 7 in English. And what is it in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5 in B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, if we look, the second paragraph from the bottom, which begins with: "The hours 430 hours on the 16th of July," then we skip that paragraph and look at the next one, "The first group went through at about 1300 hours." It is the fourth paragraph in the English version: "The first group went through at about 1300 hours and people continued going through" -- Now I've lost the text. I don't know whose mistake that was. Thank you: "People continued going through in the afternoon and during the night on 16 and 17th of July, 1995, and small groups are still passing through. For example, 33 members of the 28th Division of the KoV came through the corridor during the night of the 19th and 20th of July, 1995." "According to a rough estimate and our intelligence, a total number of," text missing. Can we please move on to the next page in the B/C/S. Thank you. Text missing. But we'll move on to the next passage, "In combat operations" -- but let me ask the question first: Is that what Beara talked about, that a unit broke through and passed through the defence lines of the VRS towards Kladanj and Tuzla? Did he tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: He told me, he actually claimed, that the majority of Naser Oric's forces had pulled out and that this unit was reviewed in Tuzla. He didn't talk in such detail as we can see in this report, but he probably had members of that unit in his mind. I cannot remember which unit he was talking about and whether Naser Oric commanded these units or some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll return to the previous page to see that Naser Oric did command them. But now I will quote the first paragraph that we can see on the page which is now in front of us. It says: "In combat operations with the 28th Division and the 24th Division of the KoV, the aggressor suffered significant losses. Twenty bodies of enemy soldiers stayed behind in our territory, and according to aggressor's reports intercepted by the PEB," that is counter-electronic struggle, "they took 30 bodies back to the Zvornik hospital. Six people enemy soldiers were captured as well as a self-propelled gun and a tank which were immediately introduced in combat against the aggressor. Another self-propelled gun and ammunition depot were set on fire in Baljkovica village." Can we see from this that there was really fighting going on in the place for which Beara said that they had pulled through -- that they broke through and pulled through, the majority of them, to the territory that was under their control?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: Well, not even the Muslim media denied that fighting was going on. As far as I understood, they say when they quote their military commanders -- I believe that even Naser Oric said in an interview that they pulled out and fought along the way. Now what exactly the fighting implies, I wouldn't know. I cannot talk about something if I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic. This is why I won't be asking anything else about that. I just told you that I would show you a part which shows that Naser Oric was involved in this and that he commanded a part of the units which were going from Tuzla. I cannot find that at the moment, so, in order not to waste time, I will ask my assistants to find that. It is not even so relevant because you said you cannot know something if you haven't been somewhere. Can we now please see 1D55 [as interpreted]. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the accused please repeat the reference, because we are not certain about the document number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you referring to D155 or to 1D55?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D155. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is correct. This is on your list of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is also a document from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated the 16th of July, 1995, "Report on the situation in Srebrenica." It was submitted after the fall of Srebrenica to President Alija Izetbegovic. Can we please see page 4 in English and page 3 in Serbian. We'll only look at one page of this document and read out one paragraph. We can see it now. In Serbian, it's the last paragraph on page 3. It's marked here as paragraph 3. And it reads: "Units of the 28th Division of the KoV are pulling out of Srebrenica while still fighting. They have remained compact. They have scored success after success in the temporarily occupied territory. They have inflicted great losses on the aggressor. So far, they have eight Chetniks (alive) in captivity. Units of the 28th Division of the KoV have linked up with the infiltrated units of the 2nd Corps. Their joint forces have continued fighting in the temporarily occupied territory. It is expected that they will fully link up with these units. Activities are underway to exploit the success of units carrying out the break-through." And now can we just please show the last page of this document - it is page 5 in this document - so we can see the signature. Thank you. We'll see a signature soon, both in English and Serbian version. It says "Commander, Army General Rasim Delic."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As you have now seen what the Muslims said about this, did Beara lie to you when he said that the majority managed to break through? Do the Muslim reports from the time say the same thing?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: I have no reason not to trust official documents, especially when they were signed by the general of an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
