utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please show D38. Thank you. We can see the document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 10, that is to say, 11, line 22, the Prosecutor asked you whether he told you what happened with the men and why they were not transported together with the women, the elderly, and the children. Mr. Tokaca says here in the title of this document, "We found 500 people from Srebrenica who are alive, although they were listed as missing." My question is this: During last year and this year, were there many articles in the press about what Tokaca said at press conferences in the territory of Republika Srpska, rather than in the Muslim territory; and do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: Yes. Some news agencies carried this information. It was brief from a press conference, I think the "Beta" news agency carried it, but I don't remember the numbers. As for those who have been found alive, fortunately, there was a lot of talk about that in the media in connection with election lists because in Bosnia-Herzegovina, names of people who had been declared killed and perished in the Srebrenica operation figured on some of these lists, and it created quite a negative impression on the people. Mr. Beara also talked about it in a brief section of the interview, if my memory served me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now look at the third paragraph of the article which we see in front of us. It says: "The biggest problem in BH is the perfidious monopoly on information, Tokaca said, pointing out that the IDC wanted to break this monopoly by compiling the Bosnian crime atlas." This is my question: When Tokaca mentioned this information that 500 people from Srebrenica who were alive but had been listed as missing, was that his attempt to break this monopoly? And do you know anything about this monopoly over information in Bosnia and Serbia because you, yourself, said a while ago that one would report one thing and others would report other things. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think, Mr. President, that there is evidence in this case with respect to this article, in the form of either a retraction or a correction, that Mr. Tolimir has not put to this witness as making representations concerning what Mr. Tokaca -- what has been attributed to Mr. Tokaca, with full knowledge of the fact that there is such information in the record. I think the questions as put to this witness are therefore misleading, and to the extent that General Tolimir -- I understand that it is P1370. And to the extent that Mr. Tolimir, or General Tolimir, wishes to pursue this line of questioning, I think it is only fair and appropriate that he put to the witness what, in fact, the record shows concerning what Mr. Tokaca has said about these missing individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document on the screen, if I'm not mistake, was gained from the Internet. It was published at the 31st of March, 2010. It's not a very long time ago. Mr. Simic, have you ever seen this article in the Internet or somewhere else? Did you read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I just know that several times from Banja Luka, and from Bijeljina, I'm not sure, there is an association of veterans in Republika Srpska. In their organisation, searching for the missing persons, they provided information that they managed to find some people who had been considered dead. But who it was, I haven't read this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should take into account that testifying about this article, the witness has no knowledge about it. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I asked the witness if he, as a journalist, felt he had a monopoly on information, and whether such monopolies are still in place in the different ethnic communities and on different sides which had waged this war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, can I only speak of Serbia and Montenegro for a while, while we were still in a common state. There was a monopoly in place. In certain situations, it was so strong, it was terrifying. Fortunately, there is less and less of it now, and many things surface much more easily. I don't think the monopoly is as strong as it had been, if you have in mind the monopoly of certain political structures and the media that is used to cover up facts about events, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have a technical problem again. The transcript in e-court doesn't work. It stopped at page 51, line 5, but LiveNote is still working. Just for the record. You may continue, Mr. Tolimir. We will not lose anything on the record, but it may be problematic and difficult to look at a document and, at the same time, on the transcript. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 29, you said: "That is true, what he said. That figure was gradually reduced to the figure of up to 7.000 people because they started off with 14.000." That is why I asked you whether, even today there is a certain monopoly in place which prohibits the public from knowing the exact number of victims in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: I can't say that certain monopoly toys with that figure of 7.000 people having been killed there. But it is a fact that there are individuals who openly doubt that figure. Of course, I still had no occasion to see any proof on which anyone would say that there were less than 7.000 victims. Many documents are still not available to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was informed by Mr. Registrar that there are, indeed, at the moment some technical problems with e-court. If you don't have a problem with that, Mr. Tolimir, you may continue. Otherwise, to re-start the whole system during the break, we need a break. Otherwise, it can't be set up again in a proper way. We could have our second break now to re-start the system, if that would be convenient for both parties. But you may continue as well. It's your decision. We have the full transcript, of course, in LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have only one question left, so it will be as you please. Following that question, I will conclude my examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, you said that you saw no proof of that figure of 7.000 or less. Did you see any proof of any other figure? Or is this a brush-stroke figure that figures in the media?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: Well, what amounts to proof? If my opinion is relevant in any way here, such proof ought to be put forth by a competent commission. Perhaps an international commission which would come up with the list of all those who were killed. It is a fact that different figures were in circulation. Even the Sarajevo media occasionally reported on people surfacing who had been considered missing or killed or buried in one of the mass graves. Those people showed up and voted. I remember such reports a few years ago in a Belgrade paper. Maybe there is such a list somewhere, but I have never seen it. I'm not aware of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic, for having come here to The Hague Tribunal to testify. Thank you for everything. I wish you a safe journey back home, and may you live a long and happy life.

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this concludes our examination of this witness. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Vanderpuye, your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would ask if we could take the break now. I just want to review something very quickly in the transcript. And I'm afraid that if e-court is not running, I may not be able to do what I need to in redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's fine. We understand that we should adjourn for the second break and resume 20 minutes before 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, your re-examination please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I only have one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You stated in response to General Tolimir's last question to you that you had heard various figures for the number of individuals that had been killed, recovered from mass graves, different figures from different sources. And you said: "Well, what amounts to proof?" And, "If my opinion is relevant in any way here, as [sic] such proof ought to be put forth through a competent commission. Perhaps an international commission which would come up with the list of all those who were killed." If you recall that answer. Let me ask you: Have you heard the figure of 5.777 individuals recovered from mass graves and identified by the International Commission of Missing Persons through DNA analysis? Has that number come up? Have you heard that reported?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: Yes, I heard of that figure. And that is why I said that such a list ought to be compiled. In spite of the fact that this official figure was published, still, in certain circles, in certain broadcasts on TV, we hear different numbers coming from NGOs or organisations. Nobody says 5.777. People usually go up to 7-, 7.500. So this official data is not frequently referred to. That's what I was trying to say. I didn't mean to say that there is no definitive list. I know there were exhumations, DNA analyses, et cetera. But even though this figure of 5.700 [as interpreted] exists, frequently, other figures appear, such as you could see in the media surrounding Mladic's arrest, and there they mention 7- up to 7.500 victims. And it is no laughing matter. It's not a game that one could play. Even a single victim is one too many, let alone 7.000. Out of respect for those victims, we should have a set figure that everyone should always refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Of course, you understand that the identification through DNA testing is an ongoing process, and the number I have given you is as of February 2010. So you might imagine that that number would increase over time?

utterances.speaker: I just checked the transcript and your answers you were -- have
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, this concludes your examination here in this trial. The Chamber would like to thank you that you were able to come to The Hague again and provide us with your knowledge. Now you are free to return to your normal life and normal activities. Thank you very much again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Thayer. While you are preparing yourself for the next witness, the next witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, welcome to the courtroom. Please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. The Prosecutor, Mr. Thayer, is now conducting his examination-in-chief. Mr. Thayer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you Your Honours. Good afternoon to the Defence. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ljubomir Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you were born, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: On the 27th of September, 1939.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And please tell us where you were born and raised.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The village of Malesevci, the municipality of Ugljevik. I was raised in the village of Brodac, in the municipality of Bijeljina, and in Sremska Raca which is in the municipality of Sremska Mitrovica. I was an orphan and I lived in different orphanages.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And sir, where do you live now, please?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: In Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You testified in this very courtroom, I believe, in July 2008, as a witness for the Beara Defence. Have you had a chance recently to listen to that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe the witness's answer, whereby he stated where he resides now, is not in the transcript. It should be immediately following line 10 on this page, but there is answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's correct. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think we all heard it. I assume it will be picked up, but I can ask it again for the sake of the record. Sir, the record, for technical reasons, doesn't reflect your answer to my question earlier which simply was, where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I live in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Turning back to your --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Turning back to your testimony in 2008. Is there anything you'd care to correct, add, or subtract from it before we move on to your testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps there is an need to correct something. In the record, there's a mention of the 38th Brigade which ought to be the 38th Partisan Division. Also, something needs to be clarified in that testimony when it comes to the work of the commission prior to my appointment as president. There is a difference in that the former president of the exchange commission was answerable to the corps commander, and he submitted his proposals to him. Then such proposals were forwarded to the Main Staff. When I arrived, the corps commander delegated some authority to his chief of security. And I was part of the security department. Therefore, I no longer had to communicate with the corps commander as my predecessor did. I communicated with the chief of security, who then forwarded information to the commander along the command and control lines, and then on to the Main Staff. That is the difference. There was another thing that was not clear enough. As regards the events in Batkovici before the 15th of March, that is to say, prior to my arrival and after, they are two different periods. I cannot address specifically the issue before my arrival. Probably, the situation at the beginning was not the same as the one that occurred yesterday --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Later on, interpreter's mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was something else that I wanted to add, but perhaps we can get to it later when we discuss someone getting in touch with someone else. But we can clarify that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. That is very helpful, and we will -- we will get to all those issues before too long. What I'd like to do for a few moments is review with the Trial Chamber a little bit about your educational, professional and military background. Could you tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about your education and the type of work you did, up until the beginning of the war. And then we'll pick it up from the point that the hostilities began.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I completed two years of high school in Bijeljina, and then I completed high school for teachers in Bijeljina and the teaching academy in Belgrade. I have lived in Bijeljina since 1953. For two years, I worked as a teacher, then eight years as a teacher in high school, two years as a school director. And then I left education altogether. I joined the state security. I was an operative in the service. I was in that position for a few years. Then I became an independent inspector in the public security domain. And in 1986, I was transferred to the TO as a commander because there some standing issues there that needed to be resolved. In the meantime, I became eligible for retirement from the Ministry of Interior. I could choose, and it was better for me to join the TO as commander for the next four years, following which I would be allowed to return to the Ministry of the Interior. We had an agreement in place about that, and things remained as such until 1991, when my tenure expired. I was sent to Sarajevo for a medical examination which I passed, and in keeping with a written agreement, I was supposed to go back to the ministry. However, those higher up, the Muslim and Serb authority, that is to say, the SDS and the SDA, agreed to divide the managerial positions amongst themselves. Therefore, only someone from the Serb Democratic Party or someone from the Muslim Democratic Action Party could occupy such a position. Given the fact that I was not a member of any party once the league of Communists ceased its existence, I told my superiors in the staff that I'd rather stay alone than choose the wrong parties, and I was a non-party member until there was a movement for the unified Yugoslavia. Then the Staff suggested to me that I should join it. However, it was too late to do anything, and that party was unable to do anything. It only caused further problems for the JNA. JNA officers had grave problems in Bijeljina because many districts voted for the Movement for Yugoslavia, and I was eligible for retirement by that time. This was supported by the municipality, and I eventually retired at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just so we have a clear understanding, sir, your service as an operative in state security and the public security was where, sir? Where did you perform that service? Was it in Bijeljina or was it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: In state security, it was the Tuzla centre, the Bijeljina department. Around as for public security, I worked for them in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, just so we have it clear, the TO which you referred to, which TO was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was the municipal staff of Territorial Defence, which is managed by the commander. There was also a republican and district staff, but during war operations, it is a military unit. The JNA military unit which arrives there is the one to which the TO unit is then resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my question was not as clear as it should be. It was actually much more simple. Where was the TO located that you were referring to before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: In Bijeljina. The seat of the municipal staff and the units belonged territorially to Bijeljina. There were several units with a total of about 10.000 members, who were in zone staffs, detachments, brigade, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think you had brought us up to sometime in 1991, sir. Can you just bring us along through the beginning of the hostilities and where you served after that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1991, when there was a reception for me on the occasion of my retirement, it was attended by the representative of the District Staff, the deputy commander because the commander was away. There was also the commander of the communications regiment in Bijeljina and the commander of the 38th Partisan Rocket Brigade. With these officers from Bijeljina, I had very good co-operation while I was the commander. So we knew each other well. The commander of the 38th Division, in brief conversation, because there were other guests, hinted at the need to man his division with commanding officers. Ethnic Muslim and Croatian officers had left the command so that only several officers remained. However, I told him that I had not even taken any rest. I was also aware that I would be engaged somewhere because war was looming ahead, but I did not wish to be a member of security. Several days passed and he called me for an interview, and he offered me to be the assistant commander for morale, which I accepted in the 38th Light Partisan Division. However, as there was no chief of security, I was in the situation to discharge both duties. I then asked that someone be found for one of the two positions so that I would discharge only one of the duties. As it was easier to find an assistant commander for morale, I took that on myself, and I selected an operative from the municipal TO staff that was a professor of defence, Ivanic. I nominated him for this position, that was accepted. And at the time when I got there, war operations had not yet begun in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The corps was located in Tuzla in 1991. In February 1991, I was in Tuzla and I took a platoon of soldiers to be trained as military policemen. I brought them back, and it was only on the 1st of April that combat operations began in Bijeljina. In order to have a clearer picture of certain issues, let me say the following: In this area, which, in the Second World War put up strongly resistance to fascism, almost everyone was on the side of the People's Liberation Army. Now in peacetime, officers were highly esteemed, officers of the JNA, regardless of their ethnicity. However, at the outbreak of the war, as in some villages that were economically strong, and one side lost the elections, there was this negative feeling towards the JNA. And therefore some officers were removed from their positions. Politicians were appointed. And then at the beginning of the war, some of them were returned. This was reflected on the lives of these officers, because the political circles called them cowards or traitors because they had withdrawn from Croatia and Slovenia, and so. And I want to say that it was very difficult -- a very difficult time for active personnel. A division commander went with me wherever I was going, and I was saying, Wait a minute. I am a reserve officer. I am a man just like you. And I wanted to say that it was not true that anyone had betrayed his own people, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I waited for the conclusion of this lengthy answer. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 62, line 1, the 38th Partisan Rocket Brigade is mentioned. And on the same page, in line 12, the 38th Light Partisan Division.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Infantry division, yes. There's no brigade. There's no rocket. It's just a division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to wait until you get the floor. It is difficult for the record if everybody is talking at the same time. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask Mr. Prosecutor to clarify the issue, because it seems that there was wrong interpretation. It seems that it was the 38th Light Partisan Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now that we've come to the end of the answer, I will follow up with a couple of brief questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, in -- in your initial answers to my questions about whether you had any corrections or changes to make to your prior testimony, you mentioned that there was a brigade that you referred to which was actually a division. Can you tell us, you referred to a 38th Partisan Unit, in which you served. Can you tell us what exactly that unit was? It's been interpreted a couple of ways. If you could just tell us, for the record, what that unit was, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The 38th Light Partisan Infantry Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, before we move a little bit further, again, I don't know if you've finished telling us about the exact role in which you served in the 38th Light Partisan Infantry Division. But can you tell us exactly what your position was, and did the division change its name at some point; and, if so, did you stay with it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: In the 38th Division, I was initially the assistant commander for morale, and I discharged also the duties of chief of security. After perhaps two months, I was appointed chief of security, because I found another suitable person who was appointed the assistant commander for morale. As the command of the Yugoslav People's Army had sent a dispatch in April - I'm not certain about the exact date - it was addressed to all subordinated commands in Bosnia and Herzegovina to the effect that all active-duty officers who wanted to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina should do that. I think the date mentioned was the 20th of May, 1992. The division commander showed me the dispatch, but officers were not informed about it immediately. It was rather only several days before the deadline expired, so that the few remaining active-duty officers left the division. There was only one warrant officer who remained. Others left for Serbia. The division ceased to exist, and therefore the corps officially disbanded it. I was transferred to the 17th Partisan Brigade. After two or three months, it was renamed as the 1st Semberija Brigade. I was also chief of security in that brigade. The brigade went to Majevica mountain, where it had a zone of responsibility. At the time, relations between the Tuzla Brigade and our 1st Semberija Brigade were very good. Combat operations were rare, perhaps a few provocations. When I say the relations were good, I mean that the soldiers from the Federation, the Muslim units and soldiers, would meet the Serbian soldiers between the lines, and sometimes with a bottle of an alcoholic drink they would talk about the new times. There was also the case where two battalion commanders from our army, the Serbian army, and from the Muslim army, also met between the combat lines. Several times it happened that some special units came to the area and carried out provocations against our forces, so as time went by, the friendship disappeared, and the situation was disrupted. I was discharging this duty in this brigade until the 15th of March, 1993. On that date, I was transferred to the corps; that was the Eastern Bosnia Corps. And I was transferred to the Department of Security as a security clerk. That was my duty. I was told that I was sent to the department but that my main duty would be the exchange of prisoners of war as a member of the commission. I was supposed to ensure that everything would be done properly, that there should be no trade, no deceit, or nothing of the sort. I also needed to check how our security conducted themselves because they were sometimes willing to trade. I had to ensure that everything would be carried out properly. At the very beginning, I was told to go to Batkovici, where the collection centre was located. I was supposed to see what the situation was like in Batkovici, to review the documents and files, to make a sketch of the facilities where persons were accommodated, and the whole area. I did that. I reviewed documents and files for several days. I made an Official Note. And I noted some shortcomings which I observed and which had existed prior to my arrival. Namely, some people were allowed to leave to visit their relatives but it was not mentioned who the relatives were, what was their address. There were cases when individuals would take certain groups away from there and exchange them privately because these were not soldiers, even though everything that happened at the time was ascribed to the military. Even if civil persons did some dishonourable things, they did it in uniform, but the army did not participant in that. The army did not take part in such incidents when people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me stop you right there, if I could, sir. And we'll talk about the Batkovici collection centre in a little while. Let me go back just a little bit. You told us that in March of 1993, you were transferred to the security department of the Eastern Bosnia Corps. Did you, in fact, have a -- an office or a desk in the Eastern Bosnia Corps Command when you began serving there, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: At the security department, I did not have a separate office. There was one room where the communications centre of the department was located. People who needed to see the chief were received there. I did not have a separate room, but I had a safe in which I could keep certain documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during your service in the security department of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, you referred to this communications centre of the security department. Where would you report for duty when you were serving in the department?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I reported to the department, which was separated. The corps was not situated in one building but in a number of buildings. There was a privately owned building where the security department was. So it's called the communications centre. The communication was there, but it was a room where the officer on duty was and he actually discharged some duties through the main communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And to whom would you report, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I reported in the morning, at 7.00 a.m., and as the office of the chief was right across, a little before 7.00, or at 7.00, the chief would invite us to his office to brief us if there was something that was common. And then, individually, he would brief individuals about what was necessary, and we would most often drink coffee during the briefing, and we would agree about the following documents that needed to be discharged.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you referred to the chief, who is that, sir, if you could tell the Trial Chamber the chief's name, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: On my arrival, it was Lieutenant-Colonel Pero Jakovljevic. He was retired as lieutenant-colonel. And when the war broke out he rejoined the service. He served in security structures in the army earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point, did Lieutenant-Colonel Jakovljevic leave the Eastern Bosnia Corps and be replaced by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know, I don't remember when exactly that happened. I think it was in late 1993. He left, or, rather, was retired again, and an active-duty officer replaced him. It was also a lieutenant-colonel, Milenko Todorovic. He had worked for security earlier. One could maintain excellent co-operation with him, as opposed to this Jakovljevic, who was rather stiff and did not often have much understanding. At one point when I said that if anyone was beaten in Batkovici that I would not be the chairman of the Commission for Exchange and told him that he would go to Majevica, I was told that I was crazy, that people lost their lives there. But I really had a mind to leave. But from my arrival there and while he was chief of security, no one was maltreated there. It didn't happen. I occasionally went there. While he was the chief, I would talk one-on-one with individuals to see how they were treated, to check that money was not taken from prisoners, that they did not have to pay higher price for anything, because, for example, they would buy cigarettes for prisoners if they had any money, and generally how the guards treated them. These persons did not treat the prisoners properly. And I reported on that. Why didn't they do that? Because some persons were hidden there. They were party favourites so that they wouldn't go to war. They wanted to represent themselves as big Serbs and patriots, but once these problems were noted, I think it was when Todorovic was appointed, the police took over the charge of Batkovici and then the treatment was quite different because the duties were then discharged in the true military fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, when you refer to the police, are you referring to the military police taking over the charge of Batkovici or the civilian police? Just so that we have a clear record.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just two final questions on this topic before we move to your work on the POW Exchange Commission. The first is when Colonel Todorovic arrived to replace Colonel - and forgive me for my pronunciation - Jakovljevic, did you report to Todorovic as you had to his predecessor?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was like this: I always informed them when I needed to go to exchange. I informed them how the exchange proceeded, what was agreed, and the chairman of the commission, while I was just a member, had to inform the Main Staff and the chairman of the state commission by a dispatch about the outcome of the talks and also the subject of the talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And, again, we'll get to that in just a moment. My last question to you, sir, and it may sound like an obvious one, but in -- from 1993 through 1995 and the end of war, did you wear a uniform to work every day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Since the end of 1991 to the 30th of April, 1997, whenever I went, and I went all the time, sometimes I would get a day of leave, I went there in a uniform. For two years, it was M77, which was the JNA uniform. Others wore the camouflage uniforms, but they didn't have one for me. And it was all the same to me which one it would be. I also attended the exchanges and negotiations with the uniform showing my rank, while I was a member of the commission and when I was the chairman. As for my predecessor, he sometimes went to these meetings in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in July of 1995, sir, do you recall what your rank was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: In July? Which year?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I think I was a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You've already spoken a little bit about your service on the commission for the exchange of prisoners of war. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, how the commissions were set up, how you became appointed a member, and, later president, what the structure was, and so forth? And I may stop you every now and then to ask you for some more details. But if you just give the Trial Chamber an idea of how these commissions operated, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: With the beginning of combat operations, the Eastern Bosnia Corps had one active-duty officer who held the rank of major and who was in charge of this. There was no commission. He was in charge of contacting the other side so that they would resolve the problems of prisoners of war and those who had lost their lives. I'm not sure when in 1992 the commission was set up. When I was in it in 1993, it was set up by the corps commander who issued an order to that effect. The president of the commission did not have other duties. According to establishment, he was the president, and he directly reported to the corps commander. The members of the commission were a secretary, who did not have any other wartime deployment. That was her wartime position. And three of us members were from the units. If you need to hear the names, I can provide them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's okay. Thank you, sir. You told us that the corps commander issued an order to set up the Eastern Bosnia Corps Commission. Who selected the various members to serve on -- on this commission?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who nominated the members of the commission. For example, one person was from the Engineers Corps; the other from the logistics; I was from the security branch; there was another person from the Brcko who was a civilian working in the armed forces. He was there with the JNA and then stayed with the army later on. I don't know who proposed those members. I don't know whether it was someone from the morale department or the security department, or maybe together. Maybe the morale department proposed and then the other department agreed. In any case, such proposals were sent to the commander on the nomination for the different members of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. So just so we have an absolutely clear record, it sounds like, from your answer, that the nominations and the decision were made essentially by the army and not a civilian body. But please tell us if a civilian body was involved in making these final decisions about who would serve or not.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was a military commission. Occasionally, some civilian structures did have an influence when the serving civilians rotated. For example, the Tuzla Commission was a mixed commission, which had some 15 members from the different municipalities. They were in charge of both civilian exchanges, soldier exchanges, and the exchange of dead bodies. At the time of my arrival, given that my predecessor was familiar with the people from Tuzla, they also engaged in civilian exchanges, as opposed to some previous exchanges that were arranged by individuals on both sides, and then there were reactions to it on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to the Tuzla Commission, sir, is it fair to say that the Tuzla Commission was a commission on the Muslim side or Bosniak side, on the other side, so to speak, from your side, which was part of the -- connected with the VRS?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Tuzla Commission was also a military commission of the Tuzla canton. All of their members were Muslim, save for one Croat, because there is Croatian population in that area as well. In other words, it was a Federation commission in charge of the Tuzla canton.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And within the VRS, can you tell the Trial Chamber whether other corps had POW Exchange Commissions similar to the Eastern Bosnia Corps' commission, on which you served?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. The 1st Krajina Corps did, the 2nd Krajina Corps, the Drina Corps, the Herzegovina Corps, and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I don't know when they had their commissions set up, but when I started going to negotiations, those commissions were already in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in addition to these corps-level commissions, was there a state-level commission as well on the Serb side and/or on the Muslim or Bosniak side?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There was a state-level commission. Both sides had such commissions. They merged the competencies of both the military and civilian part.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on your side, sir, so to speak, was there somebody who was the head of the state commission? And, if so, what was that person's name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The head of our, or RS commission, was Bulajic. I forgot his first name. The Muslim state commission, or the Muslim Croat or the Federation Commission was headed by Amor [Realtime transcript read in error "Amir"] Masovic, who is still at the helm of the institute for missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, line 73 [as interpreted] line 22, we have an incorrect name in the transcript. And it should be Amor Masovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is what I heard in the interpretation. Thank you. But it was not line 73, but page 73. Thank you. Mr. Thayer please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Mr. Bulajic, was he military or civilian, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: He was a civilian. He was in civilian clothes. He was a bad chairman.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At some point during your service on the commission, did you become president of the Eastern Bosnia Corps Exchange Commission? And if you can remember approximately when that was, if it, indeed, happened, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I must say you've got my curiosity peaked a little bit. If you can tell the Trial Chamber, since you mentioned it, Mr. Bulajic, you noted that he was a bad chairman. And I don't want to spend too much time unless you think it's pertinent to your testimony. But if you could share with the Trial Chamber why you said that. I'm just following up. As I said, you've kind of piqued my curiosity with that comment. However much detail you are comfortable providing us.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was my impression, and I believe it was correct from the outset, that he was a man of politics who was more interested in -- in individual private exchanges than in what the Serb people needed. This proved to be correct later on in some exchanges. Once he was removed, he became a wanted person. The Serb side wanted him, but he fled. When I became president, I no longer sent my requests or proposals to the president of the state commission. Instead, I sent them to the command of the Main Staff. Before that happened, my proposal was checked and discussed by the chief of the security. Next, we sought approval from the corps commander, and then it was sent up the security chain. As far as I was informed, they always sent a copy to the president of the state commission though. He never assisted any of our exchanges. And when an important exchange was to occur, I advised him not to show up. We managed to do our best, given the circumstances, in order to alleviate the suffering on both sides, to have people brought back to their dearest and nearest. There was some mutual understanding and discussion. At the outset, things didn't work out that well. For example, sometimes they would use pejorative terms for the Serb soldiers. They would say Serbian Chetniks. And I always steered clear of such names for the Muslim side, so I referred to them as Muslim soldiers or fighters. The other members of that commission attacked their president because he did it in such a way. For example, there was an attack on a Serbian settlement when the list came with the determination aggressor, Serb soldiers, I said that one cannot be an aggressor in one's own territory. It was a Serb territory inhabited for Serbs for centuries. Such methods then were stopped, and from that moment on, our relationship was a fair one without insulting. There were no longer any attempts to play tricks, and I believe the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be far happier if they had such politicians nowadays. We didn't -- we never turned a blind eye. We always tried to do our best, and I must say that they had people up their chain as we did, too. I always prepared three different drafts of documents for exchanges. There was always the original list and then lists with potential changes, if the other side refused the original one. And it was usually approved by those superior to me. I tried to save as much time as possible by doing so, by making such proposals on the spot, and it usually worked. If you're interested in what the documents say, the exchanges took place between the front lines. There would be a cease-fire on both sides, and then we moved into no man's land. We were frequently accompanied by ICRC representatives who were always interested in those exchanges as well as in Batkovici. We had an exceptionally good co-operation, mutual co-operation. They helped us with medical supplies in our reception centre. They also provided toiletries, et cetera. And they were basically there on a weekly basis. They were never prohibited from coming, unless someone was absent. Then we would always talk about a later date. We also visited each other. When I was appointed commission chairman, I had my office in town. That is to say, my predecessor had an office in town, so that he wouldn't be challenged on the street by those who had their relatives missing. They always had to go through their respective commission presidents. Irrespective of the fact that the civilian authorities disliked me because I had been a Communist, or, rather, a member of the party, there came such a time when the Municipal Deputy Speaker, Mr. Simic, the late Mr. Simic, came to the municipality asking that I be in charge of civilian exchanges as well, because some things that were happening did not amount to proper exchanges. There were many shortcomings. And he and the municipal president went to see the corps commander. They came back to me then, stating that the corps commander agreed to their proposal. However, I rejected it by saying that I was a soldier, and that I would only exchange soldiers, my soldiers for other soldiers. I also said that if I were to take up this other task I would be unable to deal with my first duty properly, and I suggested to find someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a precision question. I would just like to clarify something you said. You said that there were exchanges of prisoners, and this would take place on -- between the front lines, so in the no man's land. And this is when the -- when there was a cease-fire. The procedure seems to me to be a little odd, because usually the exchange of prisoners usually happens after a battle. So, in your situation, where you were exchanging prisoners, was there a clause, for instance, in your agreements which stipulated that exchanged prisoners could no longer fight, or were they free once they would go back to their side to take the weapons and to go back to the front line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was well-known that they were not to fight anymore, although I'm not sure it was always honoured. There were probably deviations from that rule on both sides. There were such individual cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. Because you said that, in fact, you were only dealing with the exchange of soldiers. So if I understand correctly, soldiers would go back, would take the weapons and would go back to fight on the front line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not their obligation. On the contrary, after exchanges, they would be released to go home. However, there were individuals who still wanted to fight alongside their friends from their units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you, I just need a clarification. At page 74 of today's transcript, line 23, you are quoted as having said: "It was my impression, and I believe it was correct from the outset, that he was a man of politics who was more interested in individual private exchanges than in what the Serb people needed." Then once you -- you continued to say: "Once he was removed, he became a wanted person. The Serb side wanted him, but he fled." Can you explain why he was wanted by the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, twice I attended meetings of the state commissions at Sarajevo airport, during which we agreed about nothing. Once his arguments with Masovic stopped, it was up to them to agree whether this or that group of five would be exchanged or not. So it was their private conversation. It was my impression that it had nothing to do with the army. And in my personal contacts with him, I was given the same impression. Most of the people in charge and a number of officers were aware of the fact that he was not the kind of person who could exercise his duties properly. He was set -- they told him as much when he was removed. Instead of him, another man was appointed who was a honourable man who had been a judge, and during one of the meetings he told me, Let's talk about anything, but do not mention him to me, because I know a lot of things about him. There's no need to discuss that in any detail right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The judge who succeeded Mr. Bulajic, what was his or her name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: If I manage to recall his name, I'll tell you tomorrow. Later on, he became president of the constitutional court. After a short while at that position with the commission, he became president of the constitutional court of the RS. Yes, Rosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a couple of quick follow-up questions in the few minutes we have left tonight, sir. The prisoners from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were in the VRS's custody in your area of responsibility, where were they held? What facility?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The prisoners captured by the units of the East Bosnia Corps were held in the collection centre at Batkovici. However, there weren't many. Very few were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, we'll get to that a little bit more tomorrow, sir. And can you tell the Trial Chamber where the VRS soldiers who hailed from the East Bosnia Corps area of responsibility who were captured by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- where those soldiers were typically held, in your experience, prior to these exchanges that you've been telling us about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: In the prison in Tuzla. A unit which managed to take our soldier prisoner, usually held that prisoner for a while, while they interrogated him, following which, such people were turned over to the former district prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just to help us with the time-line a little bit, you mentioned at some point Branko Simic requesting that you also participate in exchanges of civilians. Can you just give us a year in which that happened?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was in 1994, when I was appointment the president of the Commission for Exchanges. The military commission, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And my last question for this evening: You told us how you reported to the communications centre of the security department in your -- in your corps; first to Colonel Jakovljevic and then to Colonel Todorovic. Did you also have an office in connection with your duties on the POW Exchange Commission? And, if you did, where was that located?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I wanted to clarify something. It was one thing per establishment that I was in the military security service, and another in the role of -- in the commission. I was no spy. My task was to take care of those people who were involved in negotiations on our side and those escorting them, so as not to contravene some military rules and principles. That was my task. And it basically had nothing to do with the security aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Again, I'm sorry, I -- I asked a poor question. The -- my question simply was: In your role as, first a member, and then as president of the Eastern Bosnia Corps Exchange Commission, did you have an office somewhere in which you would meet with, for example, parents or relatives of prisoners, of VRS prisoners?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was an office in town, even before my appointment as chairman. In Filipa Visnjaca Street in Bijeljina. I think the number was 14, though I cannot remember exactly. It was three or four buildings from the building where the ICRC was located. It was a suitable building because it used to be a cafe restaurant, so it had an entrance from the street. And someone was always there; if not me, then the secretary who provided information to the interested parties. Civilians would come too. Muslims came because they wanted to cross over to the other side. She was open to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think we're a little bit beyond the break for the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have to adjourn for the day. Sir, I have to inform you that you are not allowed to have any contact with either party about the content of your testimony during the break. We adjourn and resume tomorrow in the afternoon for -- 2.15 in this courtroom, number III. We adjourn.
